solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Top politician crossing lake with an agricultural worker

explanation.surface: A prime minister strolls by a lake alongside a farmhand, perhaps on a rural photo opportunity.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual lake abbreviation L will not fit; this lake is the Irish spelling of the Scottish loch.
explanation.definitionFit: A ploughman is the farm worker who drives the plough.

clue.text: Fee covering part of play rehearsal

parts.note: a play is divided into acts

explanation.surface: A theatre company is charged for an act's rehearsal time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs the three theatre words together, but 'part of play' is its own chunk, ACT, and 'rehearsal' sits apart as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Practice is rehearsal: going over something to get it right.

clue.text: Attack where film stars may be working

definitions.meaning: an old word for an assault or charge

definitions.text: where film stars may be working
definitions.meaning: two words: the place where filming happens, with the preposition before it

explanation.surface: An assault breaks out on a location where film stars are shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration shows one word, but the second reading needs a space inserted: actors work on the film set. 'Attack' is the older sense, as in the first onset of the enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: Onset once meant an assault, the opening charge against an enemy.

clue.text: Naivete displayed by politician meeting head

parts.note: a member of the Green Party
a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbours Dungeness and Sheerness

explanation.surface: A politician's naivety shows when meeting the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is geographic, not the boss: a ness is a headland, familiar from place names such as Dungeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Being green means being inexperienced and naive, so greenness is naivety.

clue.text: Married sailor outside home in charge of hired vehicle

explanation.surface: A married sailor waits outside his house while in charge of a rented car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' puts AB at the far end rather than wrapping anything; a minicab is a British taxi booked by phone rather than hailed.
explanation.definitionFit: A minicab is a car hired with its driver, like a taxi.

clue.text: Brought up a new perfume in early stages of development

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing up means reading from the bottom

explanation.surface: Someone raised on a new perfume brand in its launch phase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' reads like the past of rearing a child; in a down answer it flips the letters beneath it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Nascent means just coming into being, still in early development.

clue.text: Garden pest a Greek character finally identifies

parts.note: phi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A gardener's mystery solved: a Greek man at last spots the bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' sounds like a person from Greece; it is the letter PHI.
explanation.definitionFit: An aphis is an aphid, a sap-sucking insect such as greenfly that damages plants.

clue.text: Scope of opening move, no good to begin with

indicators.note: remove G (good) from the start

explanation.surface: A chess player judges how far an opening can reach, though it starts badly.
explanation.walkthrough: A gambit is a chess opening that sacrifices a piece; with its opening G gone it leaves AMBIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean the range or bounds within which something operates, as in the ambit of a law.

clue.text: Formidable woman's uncle shakily penning article

parts.note: her is the possessive used for a woman

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the rearranged letters hold the article
shakily means unsteadily, so the letters of uncle wobble into a new order

explanation.surface: A formidable woman's elderly uncle writes an article with an unsteady hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' looks like writing but means enclosing: the jumbled relative holds the article inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Herculean, after the mighty hero Hercules, means demanding enormous strength or effort.

clue.text: Adapted Tamworth accommodation was the tops

parts.note: the Tamworth is a pig breed, and pigs live in a sty

explanation.surface: Converted housing in the town of Tamworth was top of the range.
explanation.walkthrough: Tamworth is a Staffordshire town, but here it is the ginger pig breed named after it, so its accommodation is a sty.
explanation.definitionFit: Styled means shaped or adapted to a particular design.

clue.text: Passage from a place like Sheppey?

parts.note: Sheppey is an island in the Thames estuary; the question mark flags it as an example

explanation.surface: A route leading off the Isle of Sheppey in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Sheppey lies off the north Kent coast; A ISLE runs together into the church passage AISLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An aisle is a passage between rows of seats.

clue.text: Tropical tree sheltering English king twice in battle

indicators.note: sheltering means protecting inside, so the battle wraps round the other letters

parts.note: Naseby was a decisive 1645 battle of the English Civil War

indicators.note: twice says the king's letter appears two times

parts.note: R, from Latin rex, is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A tree giving cover to an English king during a battle, like Charles II hiding in an oak.
explanation.walkthrough: Naseby, in Northamptonshire, was where Parliament defeated Charles I in 1645.
explanation.definitionFit: The naseberry, or sapodilla, is an evergreen tree of the Caribbean and Central America.

clue.text: Some thought it a nice vessel once

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

explanation.surface: A few people once admired a ship, a wry nod to how the Titanic was seen before it sank.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is ironic: the Titanic was thought unsinkable, and the answer sits inside the very phrase praising it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titanic was a liner lost in 1912, a vessel of the past.

clue.text: Wax lyrical in this way visiting east Tyneside region

parts.note: Tyneside is in the North East of England

explanation.surface: Someone raves about a visit to the Newcastle area.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyneside is the area round Newcastle upon Tyne, in the north-east corner of England, so its region is named by a compass abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To enthuse is to speak with great enthusiasm, to wax lyrical.

clue.text: Financially sound PC spoke resoundingly about that heartlessly

parts.note: a police constable is a copper

indicators.note: about means around, so the loud-speaking word is placed around the letters that follow

parts.note: spoke in a loud deep voice

explanation.surface: A police officer declared loudly that a scheme was financially solid.
explanation.walkthrough: PC is not the computer but a police constable; copper is British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper-bottomed means thoroughly reliable, especially financially, from ships' copper-sheathed hulls.

clue.text: Outlook for vocal piece that's turned up on island

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece written on another sits above it, so the island comes last

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning a word up reads it from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a song is a piece of music for the voice
IS is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A forecast for a song that has appeared on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' looks like 'appeared'; in this down entry it reverses SONG into GNOS.
explanation.definitionFit: A prognosis is a forecast of how things will develop, a likely outlook.

clue.text: Found damaged gate in Rio

indicators.note: the letters are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A broken gate has been discovered in Rio de Janeiro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as the past of find; the answer needs the verb to found, to establish.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb to found, as in founding a company, means starting something that did not exist before.

clue.text: Chap from Irish county eager at first to tour North Carolina

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all the way round it, so the county and the letter circle the state

parts.note: County Clare in the west of Ireland

indicators.note: only the first letter of eager

explanation.surface: An Irishman keen to make a trip round North Carolina.
explanation.walkthrough: The county and the eager letter travel as one unit, and it is that pair, not the E alone, that goes round the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarence is a man's name, so any chap might be one.

clue.text: Healthy walk conforming to government policy

definitions.meaning: a stroll taken for one's health

explanation.surface: A brisk walk that follows the government's line.
explanation.walkthrough: The noun is an old-fashioned name for a daily health walk; the adjective means permitted by the constitution.
explanation.definitionFit: A constitutional is a walk for health; constitutional also means in accordance with a constitution.

clue.text: Vessel Cabot hired regularly when travelling

indicators.note: travelling letters move about, so the pool is rearranged
taking letters at regular intervals, every second one of hired

explanation.surface: The explorer John Cabot hiring a ship for his voyages.
explanation.walkthrough: Every other letter of 'hired' ('regularly') gives IE, and CABOT plus IE is rearranged ('when travelling').
explanation.definitionFit: An iceboat is a craft on runners that sails over ice, or an icebreaker ship.

clue.text: Goodness knows how many men put out consuming drug

indicators.note: put out means disturbed or displaced, so these letters are knocked out of their order

explanation.surface: Countless men were knocked out after taking drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: E is the usual shorthand for the drug ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: Umpteen means an indefinitely large number, more than anyone could say.

clue.text: Easy-going police department supporting port authority

explanation.surface: A relaxed police team backs up the harbour officials.
explanation.walkthrough: The PLA is the Port of London Authority; the CID is the British police's detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a temperament that is calm and hard to ruffle.

clue.text: Nothing knocked back a lot of keen descendants

indicators.note: knocking something back sends it the other way, so the word reads backwards
a lot of but not all, so the last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone downs a drink, leaving very little for keen heirs.
explanation.walkthrough: NIL is 'knocked back' to LIN; 'a lot of' EAGER is EAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lineage is a line of descent, the family descended from an ancestor.

clue.text: Doctor abandons hanging fabric — it's imitation

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so the doctor walks out of the fabric word and its letters go

explanation.surface: A doctor walks out on curtains that are fake.
explanation.walkthrough: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor, dropped from the front of DRAPERY.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun comes from to ape, copying someone the way a monkey mimics, so it names the act of imitating.

clue.text: English playwright keeping old dog

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the playwright's name holds the old letter within it

explanation.surface: An English dramatist owns an elderly hound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old dog' looks like one phrase; 'old' is O inside the playwright, and the definition is just dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A pointer is a gun dog that points at game.

clue.text: Speeds upset US opera, initially proving inappropriate

indicators.note: first letters of proving inappropriate

explanation.surface: Tempos upset a New York opera house, first seeming unsuitable.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met is New York's Metropolitan Opera; 'upset' here turns it upside down rather than annoying it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempi, plural of tempo, are musical speeds.

clue.text: Stew made by idiot in church office

indicators.note: in says the idiot is inside the church, so its letters sit within the church abbreviation

explanation.surface: A fool in the parish office cooks up a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church office' looks like one place, but 'office' here is a post or function, separate from the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after the lidded dish it is cooked in, it is a stew slow-cooked in the oven.

clue.text: A male crew in an Asian capital?

parts.note: to staff, as in man the boat

explanation.surface: A man joins a team working in one of Asia's capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' is a verb, to staff, giving MAN; Amman is the capital of Jordan, in western Asia, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Amman is the capital of Jordan, which lies in Asia.

clue.text: Attractive second husband involved in home improvements

indicators.note: the two letters become involved in, inside, the word for home improvements

parts.note: DIY is do-it-yourself, improving one's own home

explanation.surface: A woman's second husband looks good when doing jobs around the house.
explanation.walkthrough: DIY (do-it-yourself) has S and H put inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishy is informal British slang for good-looking, sexy.

clue.text: One entering offers third of beef to marinade

indicators.note: entering means going into, so the one goes inside the word for offers
a third of a word here means its third letter, not a third of its length

explanation.surface: A cook adds a third of the beef to a marinade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marinade' is used as a verb, to soak meat, and TENDERISE matches it; I enters TENDERS before E completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym by purpose: soaking meat in an acidic liquid softens its fibres, so the one process achieves the other.
